question: The container health check reported healthy for the entire outage, and it was telling the truth. What had it actually established?

options.text: That the application was serving requests to anything that could already reach it inside its own container
options.explanation: That is the whole claim. The check runs inside the container and connects straight to the process, so it never crosses the published mapping. It was answering a narrower question than the customer was asking, and answering it correctly.

options.text: That the whole request path from the customer to the application was working
options.explanation: This is the assumption that cost several hours here. The check never leaves the container, so the part of the path that was broken was never on its route.

options.text: That the application contained no defects
options.explanation: No health check establishes that, and it is not what anyone believed. The trap in this incident was subtler: the check was trusted to cover reachability, which is a different thing from correctness.

options.text: That the published address had been configured correctly
options.explanation: The published address was wrong throughout and the check stayed green, which is exactly why this incident lasted. A green check is not evidence about configuration it never touches.

question: Requests came back as an empty reply rather than as a refused connection. Why is telling those two apart worth the effort?

options.text: A refusal means nothing accepted the connection, so an accepted one that returns nothing proves something is listening and forwarding
options.explanation: Right, and it is the fork in the whole investigation. A refusal would point at a service that is not running or not published at all. Acceptance followed by silence points at a forwarding layer delivering somewhere with nothing behind it.

options.text: They mean the same thing, and only the wording differs between tools
options.explanation: They are produced at different stages of the connection and by different parties. Treating them as interchangeable throws away the most useful piece of evidence in this ticket.

options.text: An empty reply always means the application crashed while responding
options.explanation: It can mean that, which is why it has to be checked rather than assumed. Here the logs showed a process that never received the request, so nothing crashed.

options.text: A refusal indicates a firewall and an empty reply indicates a certificate problem
options.explanation: Neither mapping holds. Both symptoms have several possible causes, and the point of separating them is that they rule out different sets of them, not that each names one.

question: The fix was a single digit. What is the honest thing to raise with engineering afterwards?

options.text: That the release changed a value nobody reviewed
options.explanation: Worth mentioning, but it treats this as one careless edit. The reason it ran for hours is not that the edit happened, it is that nothing noticed.

options.text: That the health check should run more often
options.explanation: It would have passed just as often. Frequency does not help a check that cannot observe the broken layer in the first place.

options.text: That every monitoring signal was green while the service was completely unavailable, so the monitoring cannot see this class of fault
options.explanation: This is the finding worth more than the fix. A check that connects from outside the published address would have caught it in seconds. Without one, the next occurrence is also found by a customer.

options.text: That the customer should have reported it sooner
options.explanation: They reported it promptly, from several networks, having already ruled out their own connectivity. The gap was on the provider's side.
